2. Facts leading to this Rule, in brief, are that the petitioner as plaintiff instituted a suit for permanent injunction against the defendant-opposite parties. The plaintiff's case was that the defendant No. 4, the distributor agreed to give the film 'Sujan Sakhi' to the plaintiff first or ail for exhibition at Dinajpur Town and accordingly the plaintiff paid Tk. 5000/- as advance in acknowledgement of which a receipt was also granted by the distributor. The plaintiff was also given some publicity posters of the said film. It was further alleged by the plaintiff that in violation of the said agreement, defendant No. 4 had made necessary arrangement with defendants No. 1-3 for exhibiting the film in their Halls at Dinajpur town and defendant No. 1 had already obtained the print of the film for exhibition in his Hall. The plaintiff therefore alleged that he would suffer irreparable loss and his goodwill as an exhibitor would also be jeopardized if the defendants 1-3 succeed in exhibiting the film before him Hence equal suit for permanent injunction. 

 3. After institution of the suit the plaintiff filed a petition praying for restraining the defendants from exhibiting the said film in their halls by temporary injunction. Defendant No.1 appeared and filed a written objection against the plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction. The learned Munsif after hearing the parties granted ad-interim injunction on contest against defendant No. 1 and issued notice upon other defendants to show Cause. 

 4. The defendant No. 1 thereafter preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge against the order of ad-interim injunction. The plaintiff however appeared before notice was served and contested the appeal. On the prayer of the appellant, the learned District Judge dispensed with the Scull vice of not ice Uphill other defendant respondents in the appear. The defendant No. 4, the distributor subsequently appeared and supported the case of the defendant appellant before the appellate court. 

 5. The defendant's case was that the plaintiff had paid an advance of Tk. 5000/- to defendant No. 4 but there was no agreement as alleged by the plaintiff to give him the film first of all for exhibition at Dinajpur Town and further that the defendant No. 1 was a bonafide purchaser for consideration without any notice of the alleged agreement between the plaintiff and defendant No. 4. " 

 6. The petitioner has also challenged another order dated 29-5-76 passed by the learned District Judge directed the plaintiff-petitioner to deposit a sum of, Tk. 8000/- as security deposit as a condition precedent for suspending his order to enable the petitioner to move this court. Hence the present rule at the instance of the plaintiff. 

 7. Mr. Abdul Malek the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has assailed the Impugned judgment on various grounds. He has argued that the learned district Judge erred in holding that there was no contract Inasmuch as that was the main issue to be decided in the suit after taking evidence and the plaintiff has been seriously prejudiced thereby. He has further argued that the learned District Judge has taken into consideration extraneous matters which did not come within the ambit of an interlocutory proceeding, 

 8. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties No.1 and 4 has in reply submitted that the terms of the contract were yet to be settled and the plaintiff did not acquire any exclusive right to exhibit the film first of all in Dinajpur Town. He has further argued that there was no privacy of contract between the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3. 

 9. I have gone through the impugned judgment, the petition, the affidavits and have also considered the submissions made by the earned Advocates is support of their respective cases. While going through the impugned judgment I was wondering whether it was a judgment from a decree or a judgment from an interlocutory order. The learned District Judge it appears has practically decided all the issues involved in the suit and has hardly left anything to be decided by the trial court. He has found that there was no 'legal executor contract' and it was not specifically enforceable. He has further found that the injury, if any, was not irreparable since the plaintiff could be adequately compensated have money and Further that there would be no loss of good-will. These findings, I am afraid are likely to embarrass and influence the trial court, coming as it did from the appellate authority. Caution must be taken to see that anything said in such interlocutory proceeding by the appellate court do not influence or embarrass the trial. Court on issues which are awaiting final adjudication before it. In the instant case, the plaintiff has prayed for injunction on the basis of an alleged oral agreement between him and defendant No. 4. The learned District-Judge has clearly found that there was no legal contract between the parties and as such the very basis of the plaintiff's claim, I am afraid, was gone and there is hardly anything left to be decided by the trial court. In such view of the matter, I feel, that the learned District Judge has traveled beyond his judicial discretion in deciding issues which are required to be decided after taking evidence particularly when there was no written agreement. The findings and observations of the learned District Judge, therefore, should not influence the trial court at the time of hearing of the suit and the trial court should be free to decide the involved issues irrespective of the opinion expressed by the learned District Judge. 

 10. Now coming to the merits of the instant case, the principle relating to the law of injunction are more or less well settled. Temporary, injunction is a form of specific relief which is merely provisional in its nature and its sole objective is to preserve the subject matter in controversy without determining the rights of the parties and to prevent the doing of an act whereby the subject matter or the right in controversy may be endangered. In order to sustain an action for temporary injunction it is not necessary to decide in favour, of the plaintiff upon the merits as would entitle him to a decree after final hearing and he may still be entitled to a temporary injunction although his right to relief after the final adjudication may ultimately fail. It would be sufficient if it can be shown that he has a fair and arguable case to raise as to the existence of his alleged right. 

 11. In the instant case, there are certain admitted features. Admittedly, there was no written contract in the case and that the petitioner paid Tk. 5000/- as advance to the Distributor to secure his right for exhibiting the film. The plaintiff's case was that it was agreed bevies him and the distributor that he would have the first right to exhibit the film in Dinajpur town which is however denied by the distributor (opposite party No. 4). Be that as it may, I do not think it necessary or advisable to go into the question at this stage as to whether there was a complete contract or not which in the absence of a written contract can only be decided after taking evidence. But, the fact remains that there was some kind of understanding between the petitioner and the distributor otherwise the petitioner certainly would not have advanced Tk. 5000/- to the distributor white the film was under production. This fact is also borne out by the letter dated 17-5-76 from the Distributor to the petitioner. The bone of contention appears to be that whereas the petitioner claimed the first right of exhibition of the film in Dinajpur the distributor asserted that there was no such agreement and that the terms of the agreement were to be settled later. It appears from the letter dated 17-5-76 that there was an offer of simultaneous release of the film with other exhibitors from the distributor to the petitioner. Admittedly, there is no averment either in the plaint or in the application for temporary injunction that the petitioner's alleged right to exhibit the film first also barred the right of other exhibitors to exhibit the film simultaneously. It has been admitted in paragraph 5 of the petitioner's affidavit-in-reply to the counter Affidavit filed by the opposite party No. 4, that the letter dated 17-5-76 was received by the petitioner on the same day and the suit was instituted on 21-5-76. But curiously enough neither in the .plaint nor in the application before this court there is any mention of the said letter nor is there any refutation of the allegations contained in the said letter. Admittedly, the film was released in Dacca in October, 1975 but there is no averment in the plaint as to the steps taken by the petitioner pursuant to his alleged agreement to obtain the print of the fine from the distributor during the 6/7 months prior to the filing of the suit. The petitioner it appears slept over and allowed his right to lapse by default and then suddenly woke up on receipt of the said letter from the distributor who cannot be expected to keep the film on cold storage for an indefinite period. 

 12. It is pertinent to note in this connection that the plaintiff's claim is based on oral agreement. The plaintiff alleged that the terms were settled while the distributor asserted that the terms were yet to be settled. In these circumstances, without taking evidence it does not seem possible to say with any reasonable certainty as to what the terms actually are. An agreement in order to be specifically enforceable must be certain and definite. To sustain an action for injunction, the agreement must be such that an injunction at the instance of one party to prevent the breach of an agreement can also be validly granted at the instance of the opposite party or in other words there must be mutuality. In the instant case, can it be said that the distributor could also enforce the alleged agreement against the plaintiff if he, for any reason, refused to exhibit the film. The answer, in my opinion must be in the negative. Therefore, where there is no mutuality the agreement, I am afraid, cannot be enforced. Injunction being an equitable relief cannot be granted to prevent the breach of an agreement where there is no mutuality. Section 56(f) of the Specific Relief Act lays dean that an injunction cannot be granted to present the breach of a contract the performance of which would not be specifically enforced  Section 21 of the Specific Relief Act enumerates the cases of contract which cannot be specifically enforced. Of these clause (a) deals with contract for non-performance of which compensation in money is an adequate relied and clause (c) deals with contract the terms of which the court cannot find with reasonable certainty. For these and other reasons arid considering the materials now available on record., I am inclined to hold that prima facie the alleged oral agreement was not such of which the court would order specific performance. 

 13. It is not disputed that there was no privacy of contract between the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3. The plaintiff's allegation that inspire of their prior knowledge of the agreement, the defendants 1, 2 and 3 collusively made arrangements with the distributor to exhibit the film in their hall's, has been denied by the opposite parties in their counter-affidavit. The question therefore is Whether a negative covalent can be spelled out in the agreement in question which can be enforced by the court by an injunction even though the affirmative part of it could not be so enforced. Section 57 of the Specific Relief Act runs as follows: 

 14. As discussed earlier, there is no averment in the plaint or in the application for temporary injunction that the alleged agreement barred the right of other exhibitors to exhibit the film simultaneously. As such, it appears that even under the alleged agreement, the petitioner cannot deny the right of other exhibitors to exhibit the film simultaneously. Moreover, it is also not disputed that in the case of first release of a film in a particular place, simultaneous release in two or more halls is the general practice in the film trade. Having regard to these facts and circumstances, I do not think that in the present case a negative covenant can be spelled out so as to be enforced under section 57 of the Specific Relief Act. Therefore, when the positive part of the agreement cannot be enforced by an injunction because of the reasons discussed above the same object cannot be achieved by imputing an implied negative covenant in the agreement and enforce it under the provision of section 57 of the Act. It should also be noted in this connection that there is no prayer for injunction against defendant No. 4 in the plaint or in the application for temporary injunction. In these facts and circumstances, I am inclined to hold that the plaintiff petitioner has failed to make out a prima facie case for temporary injunction against the defendant-opposite parties. 

 15. Now coming to the other impugned order dated 29-5-76, it appears that immediately after the judgment was delivered the petitioner filed an application before the learned District Judge praying for stay of the operation of the impugned order for 15 days to enable him to move this Court. The learned District Judge suspended the operation of the order on condition that the petitioner would deposit Tk. 8000/- in court which in the event of the plaintiff's success in the High Court would be refunded to him, otherwise the same would be paid to the defendant. 

 16. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed appearing on behalf of the opposite parties has argued with reference to section 115 of the Evidence Act that the plaintiff having accepted the benefit under the impugned order cannot turn round and challenge the same. The learned District Judge no doubt, has the authority either to grant or reject the plaintiff's prayer but he certainly exceeded his authority when he reposed a penal condition in the impugned order. Moreover, I do not find anything to justify the condition that in the event of success the petitioner would be entitled to refund other- wise the money would be paid to the defendant opposite party No. 1, I wonder what a judge has got to do with the success or failure of a litigant. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed in support of his contention has cited the case of Shrubendra Deb Roy and others Vs. Kumarundra Deb Roy and others, reported in, A.I.R, 1959 Calcutta 19. I am afraid the case has no application to the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In the said case a conditional order was passed that on deposit of a certain amount into court the appeal would be restored to file and the amount was deposited and the plaintiff withdraw the same. It was accordingly held that the plaintiff having adopted the order and with drawn the money deposited by the other party and having received the benefit there under, cannot be allowed to challenge the same. In the aforesaid case the court had the authority to pass the order but in the instant case the order itself was passed without any lawful authority. Moreover, the Doctrine of Election which Mr. Ahmed has tried to invoke in sup port of his contentions is based on the principle that the election must be voluntary and not one under, duress or compulsion. In the instant case, the condition was forced upon the, petitioner by circumstances beyond his control and the petitioner cannot be said to have voluntarily adopted the impugned order. I, therefore, find no substance in the contention raised by Mr. Ishtiaque Ahmed. This is not only an illegal order but a highly unconscious able one which, I am afraid cannot be justified and supported by any canons of law or equity. It is well settled principle of law that a party cannot both approbate and reprobate. But the petitioner in the instant case was forced to accept under compulsion the condition it apposed by the leaned District Judge. The impugned order, in my opinion, clearly amounts to interference with the inalienable right of the petitioner to move the superior court and of obstruction in the course of Justice. I must confess that I was surprised that a senior judicial officer of the rank of District Judge should have passed such an order. It should be remembered that a court of law must act in atonal to further the cause of justice and not to frustrate or deny if. 

 19. The District Judge is directed to Refund Tk. 8000/- to the plaintiff petitioner within 15 days from the date of receipt of this order. On the prayer of the parties, it is directed that the suit be heard expeditiously and the peremptory hearing of the suit should commence within 3 months of the dare of receipt of this order by the trial court and the parties should take all necessary steps in the meanwhile to get the suit ready for hearing. The learned Advocates of both parties have assured me of their co-operation in expediting the hearing of the suit.
